title: Disks, Filesystems, and Mounting
intro: You just attached a new 100GB cloud volume to a server for database storage. It shows up as a raw block device — here's how to go from that to a usable, persistent mount.

steps.prompt: List block devices to find the new disk.
steps.fake_output:
NAME    MAJ:MIN  SIZE TYPE MOUNTPOINT
sda       8:0     50G disk
└─sda1    8:1     50G part /
sdb       8:16   100G disk
steps.explanation: sdb is the new 100GB disk — no partitions, no mountpoint yet.
steps.why: Always identify the device by size and absence of a mountpoint before formatting anything. Formatting the wrong device (say, sda) destroys the operating system instantly and irreversibly.

steps.fake_output:
Creating filesystem with 26214400 4k blocks
Writing superblocks and filesystem accounting information: done
steps.explanation: This erases anything on the device and lays down a fresh filesystem.
steps.why: This is one of the few genuinely irreversible commands in this whole game. The lsblk check in the previous step is what makes it safe — never run mkfs from memory without looking first.

steps.prompt: Create a mount point directory and mount the new disk there.
steps.explanation: The disk's contents are now accessible under /data.
steps.why: A mount done this way does NOT survive a reboot. The database would start on the next boot writing to an empty /data directory on the ROOT disk instead — silently filling it up. The next step fixes that.

steps.prompt: Get the filesystem's UUID, needed for a reliable /etc/fstab entry.
steps.explanation: The UUID uniquely identifies this filesystem regardless of device naming.
steps.why: Device names like /dev/sdb can change between reboots (especially in the cloud, when disks are added or reattached). fstab entries using UUID=... always point at the right disk.

steps.prompt: After adding the UUID line to /etc/fstab, test it by mounting everything listed in fstab.
steps.explanation: mount -a mounts every fstab entry not already mounted — a safe test that your fstab line is valid.
steps.why: A broken fstab line can drop a server into emergency mode on its next boot, which on a cloud VM often means no SSH access at all. Testing with mount -a now catches that before a reboot does.

steps.prompt: Confirm the new disk is mounted with the space you expect.
steps.fake_output:
Filesystem      Size  Used  Avail  Use%  Mounted on
/dev/sdb         98G   24K   93G    1%   /data
steps.explanation: 98G usable (filesystem overhead takes a little) and mounted at /data.
steps.why: Close the loop: verify the end state rather than trusting each earlier command silently succeeded.
